blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A power is repeated multiplication of one number by itself. The number being multiplied is the base and the small raised number is the exponent, which counts how many copies of the base are multiplied together.

A negative exponent means repeated division by the base rather than repeated multiplication, so 10-3 is one thousandth. Any base raised to the power zero is one.

Multiplying two powers of the same base adds their exponents, and dividing subtracts them.

A root is the inverse of a power. The square root of a quantity is the number which, multiplied by itself, yields that quantity. Equivalently it is that quantity raised to the exponent one half, which is the case that shows an exponent need not be a whole number.

Scientific notation writes a quantity as a number between one and ten multiplied by a power of ten.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Ten to the power three is written 103. The ten is the base. The small raised three is the exponent, and all it does is count how many tens are being multiplied. Ten to the power three is one thousand.

A quick way to read any power of ten: the exponent is the number of zeros.

A minus sign in the exponent flips it from multiplying to dividing. So 10-3 is one divided by a thousand, which is 0.001.

Multiply two powers of ten and you add the exponents. Divide, and you subtract them.

Squaring a number means multiplying it by itself. Three squared is nine.

A square root runs that backwards. The square root of nine is three, because three times three is nine. Ask it as a question. What number, multiplied by itself, gives me this one?

Some roots come out whole. The square root of 144 is 12. Most do not. The square root of two starts 1.414 and never stops. Take what the calculator gives you and round it the way the section on rounding told you to.

There is a second way to write a root, and you need it further on. An exponent of one half means the square root. So 9(1/2) is 3, the same answer, written in the language of powers.

That is worth a pause, because it breaks the rule you started with. An exponent does not have to count copies. Once one half is allowed, so is 1.6, and 101.6 is an ordinary number the calculator gives as about 40. Logarithms, two sections on, are built on exactly that.

Write a quantity as a number between one and ten, times a power of ten. Thirty-five thousand becomes 3.5 times 104.

blocks.label: Illustration
blocks.html:
Build the ladder of powers of ten yourself, in two columns, with the Indian names on one side and the international names on the other.

power written out Indian name international name
101 10
102 100
103 1,000 thousand thousand
104 10,000
105 1,00,000 one lakh
106 10,00,000 one million
107 1,00,00,000 one crore
108 10,00,00,000 ten crore
109 1,00,00,00,000 one billion

Read the gaps. A lakh is 105 and a crore is 107, so the Indian ladder steps by two powers of ten. A million is 106 and a billion is 109, so the international ladder steps by three.

Now the failure, and it is one of the commonest in real work. A spreadsheet has a column of grain tonnages in it. The column is narrow, so the spreadsheet prints one cell like this.

1.5E+06

Somebody copies the visible part into a report and writes 1.5 tonnes.

Read what the cell actually said. That E means “times ten to the power”, so the cell held 1.5 times 106 tonnes.

1.5 times 106
= 1.5 times 1,000,000
= 1,500,000

Take a lakh and multiply it by a hundred.

1,00,000 times 100
= 105 times 102
= 10(5 plus 2)
= 107
= 1,00,00,000, which is one crore

Try the other direction. Divide a crore by a lakh.

107 divided by 105
= 10(7 minus 5)
= 102
= 100

A crore is a hundred lakh.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: “The exponent is the number of zeros” is a rule about powers of ten and nothing else. Two to the power three is eight, and there is no zero anywhere in it.

points.html: A negative exponent does not make a number negative. It makes it small. Ten to the power minus three is one thousandth, an ordinary positive quantity.
Whenever a number contains an E, or a small raised number, write it out in full before you use it.
The Indian ladder steps by two powers of ten: lakh is 105 and crore is 107. The international ladder steps by three: million is 106 and billion is 109.
Write any large figure as a digit or two times a power of ten before you compare it with another.
Asked to check a colleague’s calculation quickly, check the exponents first and the digits second.
The square root of a sum is not the sum of the square roots. Work out what sits under the root first, then take the root of that one number.
An exponent does not have to be a whole number. One half means the square root, and a value in between is an ordinary number the calculator will give you.

blocks.prompt: Write each of these as a number between one and ten times a power of ten. The list: one lakh, thirty-five thousand, ten lakh, one crore, one thousandth. Then work out, using the exponent rules alone, how many lakh there are in a crore and how many thousand there are in a million.
blocks.answer:
In scientific notation.

one lakh    = 1 times 105
thirty-five thousand = 3.5 times 104
ten lakh    = 1 times 106
one crore    = 1 times 107
one thousandth = 1 times 10-3

Lakh in a crore, by subtracting exponents.

107 divided by 105 = 10(7 minus 5) = 102 = 100

A hundred lakh in a crore.

Thousand in a million, the same way.

106 divided by 103 = 10(6 minus 3) = 103 = 1,000

A thousand thousand in a million.

Notice that both answers came out of subtracting two small numbers, with no long division anywhere. That is what the notation is for.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a colleague’s note.

Daily production is 2.4E+05 units, which is about 2.4 lakh. So annual production is roughly 8.8E+07, or about 8.8 crore.

Check every step. Say which are right and which are not.
blocks.answer:
Step one is right. 2.4 times 105 is 240,000, and 2.4 lakh is 2,40,000. The same number.

Step two, the yearly figure, is right in its arithmetic.

2.4 times 105, times 365 days
= 876 times 105
= 8.76 times 107, which rounds to 8.8 times 107

Step three is wrong, and it is the naming step again rather than the arithmetic. 8.8 times 107 is 8,80,00,000. A crore is 107, so this is 8.8 crore. That part is right too.

So all three steps hold. The thing to challenge is not in the notation at all: it is the 365. Production every single day of the year, with no closure and no maintenance, is an assumption the note never states. Check the exponents, then check the assumption hiding in the multiplier.

blocks.prompt:
A square plot of land covers 2,025 square metres. Work out the length of one side.

Then do the same for a second square plot covering 2,000 square metres. Say how many digits of that answer you would be willing to write down.
blocks.answer:
A square’s area is one side multiplied by itself. So the side is the square root of the area.

side = 2,025(1/2) = 45 metres

Check it by multiplying back. 45 times 45 is 2,025.

The second one does not come out whole.

side = 2,000(1/2) = 44.72135…

The calculator will offer you eight digits. The area you were given has four. Write 44.72 metres, or say about 45 metres. Digits the question never gave you are not yours to pass on.

blocks.prompt:
Write each of these out as an ordinary number.

102    105    100    10-2    9(1/2)    144(1/2)
blocks.answer:
102    = 100
105    = 1,00,000    (one lakh)
100    = 1
10-2    = 0.01
9(1/2)    = 3
144(1/2) = 12

Two of these are worth a second look. Anything to the power zero is one, which surprises people and falls straight out of the rules. Divide 102 by 102 and the exponents subtract to give 100. Any number divided by itself is one, so 100 is one.

And 10-2 is small, not negative. It sits between zero and one.

Check the last two by multiplying back. Three times three is nine. Twelve times twelve is 144. A root is the only operation here you can check without trusting the calculator.

blocks.prompt:
Work these out using the exponent rules alone, without writing the numbers in full.

104 times 103    108 divided by 105    103 times 10-1
blocks.answer:
Multiplying adds the exponents. Dividing subtracts them.

104 times 103    = 10(4 plus 3)    = 107
108 divided by 105 = 10(8 minus 5)    = 103
103 times 10-1    = 10(3 minus 1)    = 102

The third one shows why a negative exponent is worth having. Multiplying by 10-1 is the same as dividing by ten, and the rule handles it without a special case.

blocks.prompt:
Write each of these in scientific notation, as a number between one and ten times a power of ten.

6,200    93,00,000    0.0047    1,00,00,000
blocks.answer:
Move the point until one digit is in front of it, and count how far it moved.

6,200    = 6.2 times 103
93,00,000    = 9.3 times 106
0.0047    = 4.7 times 10-3
1,00,00,000 = 1 times 107

The third moved the other way, so its exponent is negative. The last is one crore, and a crore is exactly 107.

blocks.prompt: Section 34(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 caps District Commission complaints at one crore rupees. Section 47 caps State Commission ones at ten crore. Write both in scientific notation and say, from the exponents alone, how many times larger the second is.
blocks.answer:
one crore = 1,00,00,000    = 1 times 107
ten crore = 10,00,00,000 = 1 times 108

Now subtract the exponents rather than dividing the numbers.

108 divided by 107 = 10(8 minus 7) = 101 = 10

Ten times larger. No long division, and no zeros counted.

blocks.prompt: A district serves 1.8 times 105 meals in a year. The second schedule of the National Food Security Act, 2013 sets each meal at 450 calories. Work out the total calories in scientific notation, showing the exponent step.
blocks.answer:
Put the 450 into scientific notation first, so both numbers are in the same form.

450 = 4.5 times 102

Now multiply the digits and add the exponents, separately.

4.5 times 1.8 = 8.1
102 times 105 = 107
so 8.1 times 107 calories

Eight point one times ten to the seven. That is 8,10,00,000 calories, or a little over eight crore.

Keep the label. Calories, not meals and not rupees.

blocks.prompt: A square plot covers 8.0 times 105 square metres. Write the area out in full, then work out the length of one side. Give the side to the number of digits the area gives you, and check your rounded answer by multiplying it back.
blocks.answer:
Write the area out first. That is the habit with any raised number.

8.0 times 105 = 8,00,000 square metres

A square’s side is the square root of its area.

side = 8,00,000(1/2) = 894.427…

The calculator offers more digits than the question gave you. The area was given as 8.0 times 105, which is two digits. So write 890 metres.

Now multiply back.

890 times 890 = 7,92,100

Seven lakh ninety-two thousand against eight lakh. Not the same, and that is correct. The rounding threw away the digits that would have closed the gap. A check like this tells you the root is the right size. It does not tell you it is exact.

Keep the two units apart. The area is in square metres and the side is in metres.

blocks.prompt: A value is given as 2.5E+04 in a spreadsheet cell and another as 3.0E-02. Write both out in full, then multiply them and give the answer in scientific notation.
blocks.answer:
In full first, because that is the habit.

2.5E+04 = 2.5 times 104 = 25,000
3.0E-02 = 3.0 times 10-2 = 0.03

Now multiply, digits and exponents separately.

2.5 times 3.0 = 7.5
104 times 10-2 = 10(4 minus 2) = 102
so 7.5 times 102 = 750

Seven hundred and fifty. Check it against the full numbers: 25,000 times 0.03 is 750.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

106 times 103
= 10(6 times 3)
= 1018
blocks.answer:
The step that broke is the second line. Multiplying two powers adds the exponents; it does not multiply them.

106 times 103 = 10(6 plus 3) = 109

Check it by counting zeros. Six zeros times three zeros gives nine zeros, and 1018 would be eighteen.

Why it looks reasonable: the operation between the two numbers is a multiplication, so multiplying the small raised numbers feels like the matching move. The exponents count how many copies there are, and putting two piles together adds the counts.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

two square plots are to be replaced by one square plot of the same total area
the first covers 900 square metres and the second 1,600 square metres
900(1/2) = 30 and 1,600(1/2) = 40
so the new plot has a side of 30 plus 40 = 70 metres
blocks.answer:
The third line took the two roots before the two areas were added. The square root of a sum is not the sum of the square roots.

Work out what sits under the root first.

900 plus 1,600 = 2,500 square metres
2,500(1/2) = 50 metres

Fifty metres, not seventy.

Check both by multiplying back.

50 times 50 = 2,500    the area that was asked for
70 times 70 = 4,900    nearly twice it

Why it looks reasonable: every line that contains arithmetic is right. Both roots come out whole, which makes the working look clean and finished. And splitting a sum into its parts is something you are allowed to do with plenty of operations. A root is not one of them.

The habit that prevents it: finish everything under the root sign, then take one root of one number.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

a concentration is 5 times 10-3
a second is 2 times 10-6
10-3 is smaller than 10-6 because -3 is greater than -6
so the first is the smaller concentration
blocks.answer:
The third line inverts the comparison. A more negative exponent means a smaller number, not a larger one.

Write both out and the question answers itself.

5 times 10-3 = 0.005
2 times 10-6 = 0.000002

The first is the larger, by more than a thousand times.

Why it looks reasonable: the sentence contains a true statement. Minus three really is greater than minus six. The wrong conclusion is then drawn from it. A true clause sitting next to a wrong one is harder to spot than two wrong ones.

The habit that prevents it: write the number out in full before comparing anything.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a line from a note.

Annual production is 1.2E+06 tonnes, so at 3 lakh tonnes a quarter the plant is running close to capacity.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Put both figures into the same form before comparing them.

1.2E+06 = 1.2 times 106 = 12,00,000 tonnes a year
3 lakh a quarter = 3,00,000 times 4 = 12,00,000 tonnes a year

The two agree. Annual production and four quarters of capacity are the same number, so “close to capacity” is supported: it is at capacity.

What this does not establish. It says nothing about whether capacity is the right measure of anything. It says nothing about whether production was steady across the four quarters, or whether the tonnes were produced or merely reported. Two numbers agreeing tells you the arithmetic is consistent. It does not tell you either number is true.

blocks.prompt:
In a meeting somebody says this.

We reach 2 crore people, so a rupee a head is only 2 lakh rupees.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Do it in powers of ten, which is where the slip will show.

2 crore = 2 times 107 people
1 rupee each
2 times 107 times 1 = 2 times 107 rupees
= 2,00,00,000 = 2 crore rupees

Two crore rupees, not two lakh. The sentence is out by a factor of a hundred.

The slip is that a rupee a head for a crore of people costs a crore of rupees. The unit changes from people to rupees and the power of ten does not.

What this does not establish. Nothing here says whether two crore rupees is affordable, whether a rupee a head buys anything, or whether the two crore people figure is real. It establishes that the number in the room is a hundred times too small, which is enough to stop the meeting agreeing to it.
